metadata.title: Exponential Utility Maximization in a Discrete Time Gaussian Framework

extraction_notes.note: The numbered display (2.2) is the optimization problem; kept as an equation nested in a prose problem node spanning the sentence that poses it, rather than retyping the equation fact.

The unnumbered 'verification result' of Step II is cited later ('From Step II it follows'), so it is a Level-1 claim nested in the Step II step, spanning its statement and argument; the definition of Q_D before it stays in the Step II step.

nodes.name: Probability space and risky asset $S$
nodes.statement: To formulate our main result, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a complete probability space carrying one risky asset which we denote by $S=(S_k)_{0\leq k\leq n}$ where $n\in\mathbb N$ is a fixed finite time horizon.

nodes.name: Zero interest bank account
nodes.statement: We assume that the investor has a bank account that, for simplicity, bears no interest.

nodes.name: Gaussian price increments
nodes.statement: We assume that the initial stock price $S_0$ is a known constant and the random vector $(S_1,...,S_n)$ has a non-degenerate multivariate normal distribution.
nodes.statement_short: $S_0$ is a known constant and $(S_1,\dots,S_n)$ is non-degenerate multivariate normal.

nodes.name: Mean vector $\mu$ and covariance $\Sigma$ of the increments
nodes.statement: Hence, \begin{equation*} (S_1-S_0,S_2-S_1,...,S_n-S_{n-1})\sim \mathcal N(\mu,{\Sigma}) \end{equation*} where $\mu=(\mu_1,...,\mu_n)\in\mathbb R^n$ is a constant (row) vector and ${\Sigma}\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ (as usual, $M_n(\mathbb R)$ denotes the set of all $n\times n$ real matrices) is a constant positive definite matrix.
nodes.statement_short: The increments are $\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)$ with constant mean row vector $\mu$ and positive definite $\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Precision matrix $\Lambda$
nodes.statement: Let ${\Lambda}:={\Sigma}^{-1}$ be the precision matrix.

nodes.name: Delay $D$
nodes.statement: We fix a nonnegative integer number ${D}\in\mathbb Z_{+}$ and consider a situation where there is a delay of ${D}$ trading times.

nodes.name: Delayed information filtration $\mathcal G^D$
nodes.statement: Hence, the investor's flow of information is given by the filtration $\mathcal G^{{D}}_k:=\sigma\left\{S_0,...,S_{\left(k-{D}\right)^{+}}\right\}$, $k=0,1,...,n$.

nodes.name: Trading strategy
nodes.statement: A trading strategy is a random vector $\gamma=(\gamma_1,...,\gamma_n)$ which is predictable with respect to the above filtration. Namely, for any $k$, $\gamma_k$ is a $\mathcal G^{{D}}_{k-1}$ measurable random variable ($\gamma_k$ is the number of shares at time $k-1$).
differentia: predictable with respect to the above filtration
nodes.statement_short: A trading strategy is a vector $\gamma$ with $\gamma_k$ measurable w.r.t. the delayed information $\mathcal G^D_{k-1}$.

nodes.name: Set of admissible strategies $\mathcal A_D$
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal A_{{D}}$ the set of all trading strategies.

nodes.name: Terminal portfolio value $V^\gamma_n$
nodes.statement: For $\gamma\in\mathcal A_{{D}}$ the corresponding portfolio value at the maturity date is given by $$ V^{\gamma}_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \gamma_i (S_i-S_{i-1}). $$

nodes.name: Exponential utility maximization with delay
nodes.statement: The investor’s preferences are described by an exponential utility function $$u(x)=-\exp(-\alpha x), \ \ x\in\mathbb R,$$ with absolute risk aversion parameter $\alpha>0$, and her goal is to \begin{equation} \mbox{Maximize} \ \ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-\alpha V^{\gamma}_n\right)\right] \ \ \mbox{over} \ \ \gamma\in\mathcal A_{{D}} \end{equation} where $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}$ denotes the expectation with respect to the market probability measure $\mathbb P$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize expected exponential utility $\mathbb E[-e^{-\alpha V^\gamma_n}]$ over strategies $\gamma$ adapted to the $D$-delayed filtration.

nodes.name: Exponential utility maximization problem (2.2)
nodes.statement: \mbox{Maximize} \ \ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-\alpha V^{\gamma}_n\right)\right] \ \ \mbox{over} \ \ \gamma\in\mathcal A_{{D}}

nodes.name: Reduction to risk aversion $\alpha=1$
nodes.statement: Clearly, for any portfolio strategy $\gamma$ and a constant $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $V^{\lambda\gamma}_n=\lambda V^{\gamma}_n$. Thus, without loss of generality, we take the risk aversion $\alpha=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $V^{\lambda\gamma}_n=\lambda V^\gamma_n$, the risk aversion can be normalized to $\alpha=1$.

nodes.name: Banded positive definite matrices $\mathcal S_D$
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}\subset M_n(\mathbb R)$ be the set of all positive definite matrices $Q\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ that satisfy $Q_{ij}=0$ for $|i-j|>{D}$. Namely, ${\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$ is the set of all banded positive definite matrices with lower bandwidth and upper bandwidth equal to ${D}$.

nodes.name: Symmetric matrices vanishing on the band $\mathcal T_D$
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{T}}_{{D}}\subset M_n(\mathbb R)$ be the set of all symmetric matrices $\Gamma\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ that satisfy $\Gamma_{ij}=0$ for $|i-j|\leq {D}.$

nodes.name: Optimal exponential-utility strategy under delay via banded decomposition
nodes.statement: There exists a unique decomposition \begin{equation} {\Lambda}=\hat Q^{-1}+\hat\Gamma \end{equation} where $\hat Q\in {\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$ and $\hat\Gamma\in {\mathcal{T}}_{{D}}$. The maximizer $\hat\gamma=(\hat\gamma_1,...,\hat\gamma_n)$ for the optimization problem (\ref{2.2}) is unique and is given by the linear form \begin{equation} \hat\gamma_i=\sum_{j=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ij} \mu_j -\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \hat{\Gamma}_{ij} (S_j-S_{j-1}), \ \ i=1,...,n. \end{equation} The corresponding value is given by \begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\hat\gamma}_n\right)\right]=-\sqrt{\frac{|\hat Q|}{|\Sigma|}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mu {\Lambda}\mu'\right) \end{equation} where $'$ denotes transposition and $|\cdot|$ is the determinant of the matrix $\cdot$.
conclusions: There exists a unique decomposition \begin{equation} {\Lambda}=\hat Q^{-1}+\hat\Gamma \end{equation} where $\hat Q\in {\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$ and $\hat\Gamma\in {\mathcal{T}}_{{D}}$.
The maximizer $\hat\gamma=(\hat\gamma_1,...,\hat\gamma_n)$ for the optimization problem (\ref{2.2}) is unique and is given by the linear form
The corresponding value is given by
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda=\hat Q^{-1}+\hat\Gamma$ uniquely with $\hat Q$ $D$-banded and $\hat\Gamma$ vanishing on the band; the optimal strategy is linear in past increments via $\hat\Gamma$, with value $-\sqrt{|\hat Q|/|\Sigma|}e^{-\mu\Lambda\mu'/2}$.
nodes.label: thm2.1

nodes.name: Banded decomposition of the precision matrix (2.3)
nodes.statement: {\Lambda}=\hat Q^{-1}+\hat\Gamma

nodes.name: Optimal strategy formula (2.4)
nodes.statement: \hat\gamma_i=\sum_{j=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ij} \mu_j -\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \hat{\Gamma}_{ij} (S_j-S_{j-1}), \ \ i=1,...,n.

nodes.name: Optimal value formula (2.5)
nodes.statement: \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\hat\gamma}_n\right)\right]=-\sqrt{\frac{|\hat Q|}{|\Sigma|}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mu {\Lambda}\mu'\right)

nodes.name: Deterministic optimal strategy in two trivial cases
nodes.statement: There are two trivial cases where the optimal trading strategy is deterministic. The first one is the case of no information ${D}=n-1$. The second case is where ${\Sigma}$ is a diagonal matrix, i.e. the stock increments $S_1-S_0,...,S_n-S_{n-1}$ are independent. In both of these cases we have $\hat Q=\Sigma$, $\hat \Gamma=0$ and the value is $\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mu {\Lambda}\mu'\right)$. In particular, if the stock increments $S_1-S_0,...,S_n-S_{n-1}$ are independent the optimal (deterministic) strategy does not depend on ${D}$ and given by $\hat\gamma_i=\frac{\mu_i}{\Sigma_{ii}}$, $i=1,...,n$.
nodes.statement_short: For $D=n-1$ or diagonal $\Sigma$, $\hat Q=\Sigma$, $\hat\Gamma=0$ and the optimal strategy is deterministic.

nodes.name: Explicit solution for delays $D=0$ and $D=1$
nodes.statement: ${}$\\ (I) For ${D}=0$ (no delay) the optimal strategy is given by $$ \hat\gamma_i=\sum_{j=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ij} \mu_j -\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} {\Lambda}_{ij} (S_j-S_{j-1}), \ \ i=1,...,n. $$ The value is $$\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\hat\gamma}_n\right)\right]=-\frac{1}{\left(|\Sigma|\prod\limits_{i=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ii} \right)^{1/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mu {\Lambda}\mu'\right)$$ (II) For ${D}=1$ the optimal strategy is given by $$ \hat\gamma_i=\sum_{j=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ij} \mu_j -\sum_{j=1}^{i-2} \left({\Lambda}_{ij}-\frac{\prod\limits_{k=j}^{i-1} {\Lambda}_{k k+1} }{\prod\limits_{k=j+1}^{i-1} {\Lambda}_{k k}}\right) (S_j-S_{j-1}), \ \ i=1,...,n. $$ The value is \begin{eqnarray*} &\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\hat\gamma}_n\right)\right] &=-\left(\frac{\prod\limits_{i=2}^{n-1}{\Lambda}_{ii}}{|\Sigma|\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n-1}\left({\Lambda}_{ii}{\Lambda}_{i+1i+1}-{\Lambda}^2_{ii+1}\right) }\right)^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mu {\Lambda}\mu'\right). \end{eqnarray*}
conclusions: the optimal strategy is given by $$ \hat\gamma_i=\sum_{j=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ij} \mu_j -\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} {\Lambda}_{ij} (S_j-S_{j-1}), \ \ i=1,...,n. $$ The value is $$\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\hat\gamma}_n\right)\right]=-\frac{1}{\left(|\Sigma|\prod\limits_{i=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ii} \right)^{1/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mu {\Lambda}\mu'\right)$$

the optimal strategy is given by $$ \hat\gamma_i=\sum_{j=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ij} \mu_j -\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} {\Lambda}_{ij} (S_j-S_{j-1}), \ \ i=1,...,n. $$ The value is $$\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\hat\gamma}_n\right)\right]=-\frac{1}{\left(|\Sigma|\prod\limits_{i=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ii} \right)^{1/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mu {\Lambda}\mu'\right)$$

the optimal strategy is given by $$ \hat\gamma_i=\sum_{j=1}^n {\Lambda}_{ij} \mu_j -\sum_{j=1}^{i-2} \left({\Lambda}_{ij}-\frac{\prod\limits_{k=j}^{i-1} {\Lambda}_{k k+1} }{\prod\limits_{k=j+1}^{i-1} {\Lambda}_{k k}}\right) (S_j-S_{j-1}), \ \ i=1,...,n. $$ The value is \begin{eqnarray*} &\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\hat\gamma}_n\right)\right] &=-\left(\frac{\prod\limits_{i=2}^{n-1}{\Lambda}_{ii}}{|\Sigma|\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n-1}\left({\Lambda}_{ii}{\Lambda}_{i+1i+1}-{\Lambda}^2_{ii+1}\right) }\right)^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mu {\Lambda}\mu'\right). \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.statement_short: Closed-form optimal strategy and value in terms of $\Lambda$ for no delay ($D=0$) and for unit delay ($D=1$, tridiagonal $\hat Q$).
nodes.label: cor1

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.3
nodes.statement: ${}$\\ (I) Observe that for ${D}=0$ we have the following properties: The matrix $\hat Q$ is diagonal with $\hat Q^{-1}_{ii}={\Lambda}_{ii}$ for all $i$; The matrix $\hat\Gamma$ is given by $\hat\Gamma_{ij}={\Lambda}_{ij}$ for $i\neq j$ and $\hat\Gamma_{ij}=0$ otherwise. This together with (\ref{2.4})--(\ref{2.5}) completes the proof. \\ (II) The matrix $\hat Q$ satisfies $\hat Q_{ij}=0$ for $|i-j|>1$ (i.e. $\hat Q$ is tridiagonal). Hence, from (2.2) in \cite{B:1979} $$ [\hat Q^{-1}]_{ij}=[\hat Q^{-1}]_{ji}=\frac{\prod\limits_{k=j}^{i-1} [\hat Q^{-1}]_{k k+1} }{\prod\limits_{k=j+1}^{i-1} [\hat Q^{-1}]_{k k} } \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i>j+1 $$ and from (3.1) in \cite{B:1979} $$ |\hat Q^{-1}|=\frac{\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n-1}\left([\hat Q^{-1}]_{ii}[\hat Q^{-1}]_{i+1i+1}-[\hat Q^{-1}]^2_{ii+1}\right)}{\prod\limits_{i=2}^{n-1}[\hat Q^{-1}]_{ii}}. $$ Since $\hat\Gamma\in{\mathcal{T}}_1$ then \begin{eqnarray*} [\hat Q^{-1}]_{ij}={\Lambda}_{ij} \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ |i-j|\leq 1. \end{eqnarray*} By combining the above equalities with (\ref{2.4})--(\ref{2.5}) we complete the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\hat Q$ and $\hat\Gamma$ explicitly (diagonal for $D=0$; tridiagonal inverse formulas of Barrett 1979 for $D=1$) and substitute into (2.4)-(2.5).

nodes.name: Part (I): no delay
nodes.statement: (I) Observe that for ${D}=0$ we have the following properties: The matrix $\hat Q$ is diagonal with $\hat Q^{-1}_{ii}={\Lambda}_{ii}$ for all $i$; The matrix $\hat\Gamma$ is given by $\hat\Gamma_{ij}={\Lambda}_{ij}$ for $i\neq j$ and $\hat\Gamma_{ij}=0$ otherwise. This together with (\ref{2.4})--(\ref{2.5}) completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: For $D=0$, $\hat Q^{-1}$ is the diagonal of $\Lambda$ and $\hat\Gamma$ its off-diagonal part; substitute.

nodes.name: Part (II): unit delay
nodes.statement: (II) The matrix $\hat Q$ satisfies $\hat Q_{ij}=0$ for $|i-j|>1$ (i.e. $\hat Q$ is tridiagonal). Hence, from (2.2) in \cite{B:1979} $$ [\hat Q^{-1}]_{ij}=[\hat Q^{-1}]_{ji}=\frac{\prod\limits_{k=j}^{i-1} [\hat Q^{-1}]_{k k+1} }{\prod\limits_{k=j+1}^{i-1} [\hat Q^{-1}]_{k k} } \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i>j+1 $$ and from (3.1) in \cite{B:1979} $$ |\hat Q^{-1}|=\frac{\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n-1}\left([\hat Q^{-1}]_{ii}[\hat Q^{-1}]_{i+1i+1}-[\hat Q^{-1}]^2_{ii+1}\right)}{\prod\limits_{i=2}^{n-1}[\hat Q^{-1}]_{ii}}. $$ Since $\hat\Gamma\in{\mathcal{T}}_1$ then \begin{eqnarray*} [\hat Q^{-1}]_{ij}={\Lambda}_{ij} \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ |i-j|\leq 1. \end{eqnarray*} By combining the above equalities with (\ref{2.4})--(\ref{2.5}) we complete the proof.
nodes.statement_short: For $D=1$, use tridiagonal-inverse formulas and the band equality $\hat Q^{-1}=\Lambda$ on $|i-j|\le1$.

nodes.name: Tridiagonal inverse formulas
nodes.statement: The matrix $\hat Q$ satisfies $\hat Q_{ij}=0$ for $|i-j|>1$ (i.e. $\hat Q$ is tridiagonal). Hence, from (2.2) in \cite{B:1979} $$ [\hat Q^{-1}]_{ij}=[\hat Q^{-1}]_{ji}=\frac{\prod\limits_{k=j}^{i-1} [\hat Q^{-1}]_{k k+1} }{\prod\limits_{k=j+1}^{i-1} [\hat Q^{-1}]_{k k} } \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i>j+1 $$ and from (3.1) in \cite{B:1979} $$ |\hat Q^{-1}|=\frac{\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n-1}\left([\hat Q^{-1}]_{ii}[\hat Q^{-1}]_{i+1i+1}-[\hat Q^{-1}]^2_{ii+1}\right)}{\prod\limits_{i=2}^{n-1}[\hat Q^{-1}]_{ii}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\hat Q$ tridiagonal, so Barrett's formulas give the entries and determinant of $\hat Q^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Band entries equal those of $\Lambda$
nodes.statement: Since $\hat\Gamma\in{\mathcal{T}}_1$ then \begin{eqnarray*} [\hat Q^{-1}]_{ij}={\Lambda}_{ij} \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ |i-j|\leq 1. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: $\hat\Gamma\in\mathcal T_1$ gives $\hat Q^{-1}_{ij}=\Lambda_{ij}$ for $|i-j|\le1$.

nodes.name: Combine with (2.4)-(2.5)
nodes.statement: By combining the above equalities with (\ref{2.4})--(\ref{2.5}) we complete the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute into (2.4)-(2.5).

nodes.name: No Markov assumption needed
nodes.statement: Let us emphasize that we do not assume any Markov structure for the underlying asset, hence even for the ``usual'' case ${D}=0$ Theorem \ref{thm2.1} gives an efficient way to solve a non-Markovian optimization problem.

nodes.name: Kac-Murdock-Szegő covariance with zero drift
nodes.statement: Consider a simple model where the increments have zero mean (i.e. $\mu=0$) and the covariance matrix is the Kac-Murdock-Szeg\"{o} matrix $$ \Sigma_{ij}:=\rho^{|i-j|} \ \ \forall i,j $$ for some constant $\rho\in(0,1)$. Assume that $n\geq 3$. The matrix $\Sigma$ has a determinant equal to $|\Sigma|=\left(1-\rho^2\right)^{n-1}$, and a simple tridiagonal inverse that is given by (see \cite {D:2003}) \[ {\Lambda}_{ij}= \begin{cases} 0, &|i-j|>1 \\ -\frac{\rho}{ 1-\rho^2}, & |i-j|=1 \\ \frac{1+\rho^2}{ 1-\rho^2} , &1<i=j<n \\ \frac{1}{ 1-\rho^2}, & \mbox{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] ${}$\\ \textbf{Case I: ${D}=0$.} From Corollary \ref{cor1} we obtain that the optimal strategy is $\hat\gamma_1=0$, and $\hat\gamma_i=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho^2} (S_{i-1}-S_{i-2})$ for $i>1$. The value is $-\sqrt{\frac{1-\rho^2}{(1+\rho^2)^{n-2}}} $. \\ \textbf{Case II: ${D}=1$.} Corollary \ref{cor1} gives the optimal strategy $$\hat\gamma_1=\hat\gamma_2=0 \ \ \mbox{and} \ \ \ \hat\gamma_i=\frac{1+\rho^2}{1-\rho^2}\sum_{j=1}^{i-2}\left(-\frac{\rho}{1+\rho^2}\right)^{i-j} (S_j-S_{j-1}) \ \ \mbox{for} \ \ i>2.$$ The value is $-\sqrt{\frac{\left(1-\rho^2\right)\left(1+\rho^2\right)^{n-2}}{\left(1+\rho^2+\rho^4\right)^{n-3}}}.$
nodes.statement_short: For the Kac-Murdock-Szegő covariance $\Sigma_{ij}=\rho^{|i-j|}$ with $\mu=0$, explicit optimal strategies and values for $D=0$ and $D=1$.
nodes.label: exm.1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement: The proof will be done in three steps. \\ ${}$\\ \textbf{Step I:} In this step we provide an existence and uniqueness for the decomposition (\ref{2.3}). We apply the results from \cite{BF:81} which perfectly fit our purposes. First we introduce some notations. Let $C \in M_n(\mathbb R)$ and $I,J \in \{1,..,n\}^k$ be two integer vectors of length $k \leq n$ denoting row and column indices, satisfying $I = (i_1,..,i_k), J=(j_1,..,j_k)$ with $1 \leq i_1 < i_2 < .. < i_k \leq n$, $1 \leq j_1 < j_2 < .. < j_k \leq n$. We denote by $C_J^I$ the minor specified by these indices, i.e. the determinant of the $k \times k$ sub-matrix determined by taking the elements $C_{ij}$ for $i=i_1,..i_k ; j=j_1,..j_k$. For any two natural numbers $b \geq a$ we denote the vector $(a,a+1,...,b)$ by $[a:b]$. Since ${\Lambda}$ is positive definite it follows by Sylvester’s criterion (see e.g. \cite{G:1991}) that its principal minors ${\Lambda}^{[k+1:k+{D}]}_{[k+1:k+{D}]}>0$ for all $k\leq n-{D}-1$ and ${\Lambda}^{[k:k+{D}]}_{[k:k+{D}]}>0$ for all $k\leq n-{D}$. Hence, by applying Theorem 5.5 in \cite{BF:81} for $r=s={D}+1$ we obtain that there is a unique invertible matrix $R$ such that $R^{-1}\in{\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$ and ${\Lambda}-R\in {\mathcal{T}}_{{D}}$. Set $\hat Q:=R^{-1}$, $\hat\Gamma={\Lambda}-R$. Since ${\Sigma}$ is symmetric then from uniqueness it follows that $R$ is also symmetric and the first step is completed. \\ ${}$\\ \textbf{Step II: } Denote by $\mathcal Q_{{D}}$ the set of all equivalent probability measures $\mathbb Q\sim\mathbb P$ with finite entropy $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]<\infty$ relative to $\mathbb P$ that satisfy \begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[S_t-S_s|\mathcal G^{{D}}_s]=0 \ \ \forall t\geq s. \end{equation} In this step we prove the following verification result: If a triplet $(\tilde\gamma,\tilde{\mathbb Q},C)\in \mathcal A_{{D}}\times \mathcal Q_{{D}}\times\mathbb R$ satisfies \begin{equation} V^{\tilde\gamma}_n+\log\left(\frac{d{\tilde{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)=C \end{equation} then $\tilde\gamma\in\mathcal A_{{D}}$ is the unique optimal portfolio for the optimization problem (\ref{2.2}) and the corresponding value is $ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\tilde\gamma}_n\right)\right]=-e^{-C}.$ Indeed, using similar arguments as in the proof of Lemma 2.1 in \cite{BD:2021}, it follows that for any $\gamma\in\mathcal A_{{D}}$ and $\mathbb Q\in \mathcal Q_{{D}}$ we have $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[V^{\gamma}_n]=0$ provided that $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \gamma}_n\right)\right]<\infty$. From (\ref{4.2-+}) $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{\tilde \gamma}_n\right)\right]=e^{-C}.$ Hence, $\mathbb E_{\tilde{\mathbb Q}}[V^{\tilde\gamma}_n]=0$ and by applying (\ref{4.2-+}) again \begin{equation} \log\left(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{\tilde \gamma}_n\right)\right] \right)=-C=- \mathbb E_{\tilde{\mathbb Q}}\left[\log \left(\frac{d\tilde{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]. \end{equation} Next, it is well known that for a strictly concave utility maximization problem, the optimizer is unique (if exists). Thus, in view of (\ref{4.2}), in order to complete the proof of the second step it remains to show that in general we have the inequality \begin{equation} \log\left(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{\gamma}_n\right)\right] \right)\geq -\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right] \ \ \forall (\gamma,\mathbb Q)\in\mathcal A_{{D}}\times\mathcal Q_{{D}}. \end{equation} Let us establish (\ref{4.2+}). Without loss of generality assume that $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \gamma}_n\right)\right]<\infty$ (otherwise (\ref{4.2+}) is trivial). Then for any $z\in\mathbb R$ \begin{align*} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \gamma}_n\right)\right] &=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \gamma}_n\right)+z \frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}V^{\gamma}_n\right]\\ &\geq \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[z\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\left(1-\log \left(z\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right)\right]\\ &=z-z\log z-z\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]. \end{align*} The first equality is due to $\mathbb E_{{\mathbb Q}}[V^{\gamma}_n]=0$. The inequality follows from the Legendre-Fenchel duality inequality $xy \leq e^x+y(\log y-1)$ for all $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$ by setting $x=-V^{\gamma}_n$ and $y=z\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}$. The last equality is straightforward. From simple calculus it follows that the concave function $z\rightarrow z-z\log z-z\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]$, $z>0$ attains its maximum at $z^{*}:=\exp\left(-\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]\right)$ and the corresponding maximal value is also $z^{*}$. This completes the proof of (\ref{4.2+}). \\ ${}$\\ \textbf{Step III:} In view of Step I the portfolio $\hat\gamma$ from (\ref{2.4}) is well defined. From the fact that $\hat\Gamma_{ij}=0$ for $|i-j|\leq {D}$ we obtain that $\hat\gamma\in\mathcal A_{{D}}$. Set \begin{equation*} C:=\frac{1}{2}\left(\log |\Sigma|-\log |\hat Q|+ \mu {\Lambda}\mu' \right) \end{equation*} and define the measure $\hat{\mathbb Q}$ by the Radon-Nikodym derivative \begin{equation} \frac{d\hat{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}:=\exp\left(C-V^{\hat\gamma}_n\right). \end{equation} From Step II it follows that in order to complete the proof of Theorem \ref{thm2.1} it remains to establish that the measure $\hat{\mathbb Q}$ is a probability measure which satisfies $\hat{\mathbb Q}\in\mathcal Q_{{D}}$. To that end define $X=(X_1,...,X_n)$ by $X_i=S_i-S_{i-1}$, $i=1,...,n$. From (\ref{2.4}) we have (recall that $\hat\Gamma$ is symmetric) $V^{\hat\gamma}_n=\hat\gamma X'=\mu {\Lambda} X'-\frac{1}{2} X\hat\Gamma X'$. nodes.name: Step I: existence and uniqueness of the decomposition
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step I:} In this step we provide an existence and uniqueness for the decomposition (\ref{2.3}). We apply the results from \cite{BF:81} which perfectly fit our purposes. First we introduce some notations. Let $C \in M_n(\mathbb R)$ and $I,J \in \{1,..,n\}^k$ be two integer vectors of length $k \leq n$ denoting row and column indices, satisfying $I = (i_1,..,i_k), J=(j_1,..,j_k)$ with $1 \leq i_1 < i_2 < .. < i_k \leq n$, $1 \leq j_1 < j_2 < .. < j_k \leq n$. We denote by $C_J^I$ the minor specified by these indices, i.e. the determinant of the $k \times k$ sub-matrix determined by taking the elements $C_{ij}$ for $i=i_1,..i_k ; j=j_1,..j_k$. For any two natural numbers $b \geq a$ we denote the vector $(a,a+1,...,b)$ by $[a:b]$. Since ${\Lambda}$ is positive definite it follows by Sylvester’s criterion (see e.g. \cite{G:1991}) that its principal minors ${\Lambda}^{[k+1:k+{D}]}_{[k+1:k+{D}]}>0$ for all $k\leq n-{D}-1$ and ${\Lambda}^{[k:k+{D}]}_{[k:k+{D}]}>0$ for all $k\leq n-{D}$. Hence, by applying Theorem 5.5 in \cite{BF:81} for $r=s={D}+1$ we obtain that there is a unique invertible matrix $R$ such that $R^{-1}\in{\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$ and ${\Lambda}-R\in {\mathcal{T}}_{{D}}$. nodes.name: Step II: verification result
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step II: } Denote by $\mathcal Q_{{D}}$ the set of all equivalent probability measures $\mathbb Q\sim\mathbb P$ with finite entropy $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]<\infty$ relative to $\mathbb P$ that satisfy \begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[S_t-S_s|\mathcal G^{{D}}_s]=0 \ \ \forall t\geq s. \end{equation} In this step we prove the following verification result: If a triplet $(\tilde\gamma,\tilde{\mathbb Q},C)\in \mathcal A_{{D}}\times \mathcal Q_{{D}}\times\mathbb R$ satisfies \begin{equation} V^{\tilde\gamma}_n+\log\left(\frac{d{\tilde{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)=C \end{equation} then $\tilde\gamma\in\mathcal A_{{D}}$ is the unique optimal portfolio for the optimization problem (\ref{2.2}) and the corresponding value is $ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\tilde\gamma}_n\right)\right]=-e^{-C}.$ Indeed, using similar arguments as in the proof of Lemma 2.1 in \cite{BD:2021}, it follows that for any $\gamma\in\mathcal A_{{D}}$ and $\mathbb Q\in \mathcal Q_{{D}}$ we have $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[V^{\gamma}_n]=0$ provided that $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \gamma}_n\right)\right]<\infty$. From simple calculus it follows that the concave function $z\rightarrow z-z\log z-z\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]$, $z>0$ attains its maximum at $z^{*}:=\exp\left(-\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]\right)$ and the corresponding maximal value is also $z^{*}$. This completes the proof of (\ref{4.2+}).

nodes.statement_short: $\hat Q$ $D$-banded makes $X_k$ independent of the delayed past, giving (4.2-).

nodes.name: Gaussian equivalent measures and equivalent martingale measures
nodes.statement: Observe that for any positive definite matrix $Q\in M_n(\mathbb R)$, the probability measure $\mathbb Q\sim\mathbb P$ which is given by $$ \frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}=\frac{\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}X Q^{-1}X'\right)}{\sqrt {(2\pi)^n | Q|}}}{\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(X-\mu){\Lambda}(X-\mu)'\right)}{\sqrt {(2\pi)^n |\Sigma|}}}$$ satisfies $\left(X;{\mathbb Q}\right) \sim\mathcal N(0, Q)$. In particular for a diagonal $Q$ the measure $\mathbb Q$ is an equivalent martingale measure, and so the market is arbitrage-free in the classical sense (no delay). Clearly, for any ${D}$ the set $\mathcal Q_{{D}}$ contains the set of all equivalent martingale measures.
nodes.statement_short: Any positive definite $Q$ gives an equivalent measure with $X\sim\mathcal N(0,Q)$; diagonal $Q$ yields an EMM, so the market is arbitrage-free, and $\mathcal Q_D$ contains all EMMs.

nodes.name: Derivation of the minor characterization of $\hat Q^{-1}$
nodes.statement: In view of Corollary 3.2 in \cite{BF:81} and the fact that $\hat Q\in {\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$, we look for a matrix $R:=\hat Q^{-1}$ that satisfies $R_{ij}={\Lambda}_{ij}$ for $i,j<{D}+1$ and has vanishing super and sub ${D}+1$ minors, i.e. minors of the form $R^I_J$ where $I=(i_1,...,i_{{D}+1})$, $J=(j_1,...,j_{{D}+1})$ that satisfy one of the inequalities $j_1>i_{{D}+1}-{D}$ (super minors) or $i_1>j_{{D}+1}-{D}$ (sub minors). The matrix $R$ is symmetric hence we can restrict ourselves to looking only at super minors. Since ${\Lambda}$ is positive definite and $R_{ij}={\Lambda}_{ij}$ for $i,j<{D}+1$, it follows that the principal minors $R^{[i+1:i+{D}]}_{[i+1:i+{D}]}>0$ for all $i\leq n-{D}-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 3.2 of Barrett-Feinsilver turns $\hat Q\in\mathcal S_D$ into vanishing $(D+1)$-minors of $R=\hat Q^{-1}$; symmetry reduces to super minors and positivity of principal minors is inherited from $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: Characterization of $R=\hat Q^{-1}$ by vanishing minors
nodes.statement: Thus, from Theorem 3.4 in \cite{BF:81} we conclude that the matrix $R:=\hat Q^{-1}$ is the unique symmetric matrix that satisfies $R_{ij}={\Lambda}_{ij}$ for $|i-j|\leq {D}$ and \begin{equation} R^{[i:i+{D}]}_{(i+1,i+2,...,i+{D},i+m)}=0, \ \ i\in [1:n-{D}-1], \ \ m\in [1+{D}:n-i]. \end{equation}
conclusions: the matrix $R:=\hat Q^{-1}$ is the unique symmetric matrix that satisfies $R_{ij}={\Lambda}_{ij}$ for $|i-j|\leq {D}$ and \begin{equation} R^{[i:i+{D}]}_{(i+1,i+2,...,i+{D},i+m)}=0, \ \ i\in [1:n-{D}-1], \ \ m\in [1+{D}:n-i]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $R=\hat Q^{-1}$ is the unique symmetric matrix agreeing with $\Lambda$ on the band and with vanishing $(D+1)$ super minors (3.1).

nodes.name: Minors can be ordered to determine one unknown entry each
nodes.statement: Observe that it is possible to order the $({D}+1)$-minors in \eqref{3.1} such that each minor is a function of $({D}+1)^2-1$ known elements of $R$, and one unknown element, hence providing a linear equation for this unknown element.
conclusions: it is possible to order the $({D}+1)$-minors in \eqref{3.1} such that each minor is a function of $({D}+1)^2-1$ known elements of $R$, and one unknown element, hence providing a linear equation for this unknown element.
nodes.statement_short: The minors in (3.1) can be ordered so each is linear in a single unknown entry of $R$.

nodes.name: Laplace-expansion argument for the ordering of minors
nodes.statement: For example, the first minor $R^{[1:1+{D}]}_{[2:2+{D}]}$ is determined by $(R_{ij} ), i=1,..,{D}+1 ; j=2,..,{D}+2$ which are all set to the corresponding elements of ${\Lambda}$ because $|i-j|\leq {D}$ except for $R_{1 {D}+2}$. For four integers $a \leq i \leq b \leq j$, denote by $[a:b]^{i \to j}$ the vector obtained by omitting the index $i$ from $[a:b]$, and adding in the last coordinate the index $j$, i.e. $[a:b]^{i \to j} = (a,a+1,..,i-1,i+1,..,b, j)$. Hence, in the Laplace expansion for the $({D}+1)$-minor \begin{equation*} 0 = R^{[1:1+{D}]}_{[2:2+{D}]} = (-1)^{{D}}R_{1 2+{D}}R^{[2:1+{D}]}_{[2:1+{D}]} +\sum_{j=1}^{{D}} (-1)^{1+j} R_{1 1+j} R^{[2:1+{D}]}_{[2:2+{D}]^{1+j \to 2+{D}}} \end{equation*} all the ${D}$-minors are known, and the unknown term $R_{1 2+{D}}$ appears only in the first term. It is therefore possible to express $R_{1 2+{D}}$ uniquely as a linear function of the known $({D}+1)^2-1$ $R_{ij}$ values. Once $R_{1 {D}+2}$ is determined, we can express the next $({D}+1)$-minor $R^{[2:2+{D}]}_{[3:3+{D}]}$ in terms of $({D}+1)^2-1$ known $R_{ij}$ elements and the unknown element $R_{2 {D}+3}$, and determine it in a similar manner.
nodes.statement_short: Laplace expansion of the first minor along its first row isolates $R_{1,D+2}$ with a nonzero known coefficient; repeat for the next minors.

nodes.name: Index vector $[a:b]^{i\to j}$
nodes.statement: For four integers $a \leq i \leq b \leq j$, denote by $[a:b]^{i \to j}$ the vector obtained by omitting the index $i$ from $[a:b]$, and adding in the last coordinate the index $j$, i.e. $[a:b]^{i \to j} = (a,a+1,..,i-1,i+1,..,b, j)$.

nodes.name: Banded Matrix Decomposition
nodes.statement: \caption{Banded Matrix Decomposition} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex {\bf Input:} $\Sigma \in M_n(\mathbb R)$ - a real Positive Definite matrix, ${D} \leq n-1$ - band width. \Statex {\bf Output:} Two matrices $R+\hat\Gamma={\Sigma}^{-1}$ such that $R^{-1} \in {\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}, \hat\Gamma \in {\mathcal{T}}_{{D}}$. \State Compute the inverse ${\Lambda}=\Sigma^{-1}$ and set $R_{ij} = {\Lambda}_{ij}, \forall |i-j|\leq {D}$. \For{$m={D}+1$ to $n-1$} \For{$i=1$ to $n-m$} \State Set $$R_{i+m i}, R_{i i+m} = \frac{\sum\limits_{j=1}^{{D}} (-1)^{j+{D}} R_{i i+j} R_{[i+1:i+{D}]^{i+j \to i+m}}^{[i+1:i+{D}]}}{R_{[i+1:i+{D}]}^{[i+1:i+{D}]}}.$$ \EndFor \EndFor \State Set $\hat\Gamma = {\Lambda}-R$. \State Output the matrices $R, \hat\Gamma$. \end{algorithmic}
input: $\Sigma \in M_n(\mathbb R)$ - a real Positive Definite matrix, ${D} \leq n-1$ - band width.
nodes.statement_short: Computes the decomposition $\Sigma^{-1}=R+\hat\Gamma$ by filling the off-band entries of $R$ diagonal by diagonal, each from a vanishing $(D+1)$-minor via Laplace expansion.

nodes.name: Invert $\Sigma$ and copy the band of $\Lambda$ into $R$
nodes.statement: Compute the inverse ${\Lambda}=\Sigma^{-1}$ and set $R_{ij} = {\Lambda}_{ij}, \forall |i-j|\leq {D}$.

nodes.name: Fill symmetric entry from vanishing minor
nodes.statement_short: Solve the vanishing $(D+1)$-minor for $R_{i,i+m}$ by Laplace expansion along its first row.

nodes.name: Set $\hat\Gamma=\Lambda-R$
nodes.statement: Set $\hat\Gamma = {\Lambda}-R$.

nodes.name: Output $R,\hat\Gamma$
nodes.statement: Output the matrices $R, \hat\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Computational complexity of the algorithm
nodes.statement: As matrix inversion can be performed in $O\left(n^{2.373}\right)$ floating points operations \cite{W:2011}, the total number of floating points operations for Algorithm \ref{alg:band_decomposition} is $O\left(n^{2.373}\right)$ (for matrix inversion), plus $O\left(n^2 \times {D}^{2.373}\right)$ for computing the minors (see \cite{A:1974}), hence yielding an overall computational complexity of $O\left(n^2 (n^{0.373} + {D}^{2.373})\right)$ floating point operations. When $\Sigma$ has a special structure, specialized faster algorithms can be used. For example, if $\Sigma$ is a Toeplitz matrix, inversion can be performed in $O\left(n^2\right)$ floating point operations using Trench's algorithm \cite{T:1964}, hence the overall complexity is reduced to $O\left(n^2 {D}^{2.373}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Algorithm 1 costs $O(n^{2.373})$ for inversion plus $O(n^2D^{2.373})$ for minors; Toeplitz $\Sigma$ allows $O(n^2D^{2.373})$ via Trench's algorithm.

nodes.name: Fractional Brownian motion
nodes.statement: A fractional Brownian motion (fBm) \cite{M:1968} with Hurst parameter ${\mathcal{H}} \in (0,1)$ is a centered Gaussian process $B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_t$, $t\geq 0$ with the covariance function \begin{equation} Cov\left(B^{\mathcal{H}}_s,B^{\mathcal{H}}_t\right)=\frac{1}{2} \left(t^{2{\mathcal{H}}}+s^{2{\mathcal{H}}}-|t-s|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}\right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: fBm covariance
nodes.statement: Cov\left(B^{\mathcal{H}}_s,B^{\mathcal{H}}_t\right)=\frac{1}{2} \left(t^{2{\mathcal{H}}}+s^{2{\mathcal{H}}}-|t-s|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}\right).
nodes.label: eq:fbm

nodes.name: Discretized fBm market
nodes.statement: We consider a discretized version of the fBm framework. Namely, we fix ${\mathcal{H}}\in (0,1)$, a time-resolution $\Delta t > 0$ and a final time $T=n \Delta t$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$, and consider the fBm market which is active at times $0, \Delta t, 2\Delta t, \dots, n\Delta t=T$.

nodes.name: Stock price in the discretized fBm market
nodes.statement: The stock price at time $k \Delta t$ is given by $S_k=S_0+B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{k \Delta t}$, $k=0,1,\dots,n$.

nodes.name: Toeplitz covariance of discretized fBm increments
nodes.statement: In this case $\mu=0$ and by \eqref{eq:fbm} the covariance matrix is the Toeplitz matrix given by \begin{align} \Sigma_{ij} &= Cov\left(B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{(i+1)\Delta t}-B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{i \Delta t}, B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{(j+1)\Delta t}-B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{j\Delta t}\right) \nonumber \\ &=\frac{\Delta t^{2{\mathcal{H}}}}{2} \left(|i-j-1|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}+|i-j+1|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}-2|i-j|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}\right). \end{align}
conclusions: $\mu=0$ and by \eqref{eq:fbm} the covariance matrix is the Toeplitz matrix given by \begin{align} \Sigma_{ij} &= Cov\left(B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{(i+1)\Delta t}-B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{i \Delta t}, B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{(j+1)\Delta t}-B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{j\Delta t}\right) \nonumber \\ &=\frac{\Delta t^{2{\mathcal{H}}}}{2} \left(|i-j-1|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}+|i-j+1|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}-2|i-j|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}\right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The fBm increments have zero mean and Toeplitz covariance $\frac{\Delta t^{2H}}{2}(|i-j-1|^{2H}+|i-j+1|^{2H}-2|i-j|^{2H})$.

nodes.name: Discretized fBm covariance
nodes.statement: \Sigma_{ij} &= Cov\left(B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{(i+1)\Delta t}-B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{i \Delta t}, B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{(j+1)\Delta t}-B^{{\mathcal{H}}}_{j\Delta t}\right) \nonumber \\ &=\frac{\Delta t^{2{\mathcal{H}}}}{2} \left(|i-j-1|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}+|i-j+1|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}-2|i-j|^{2{\mathcal{H}}}\right).
nodes.label: eq:fbm_discrete

nodes.name: Positive definiteness of the discretized fBm covariance
nodes.statement: By following carefully the proof of Proposition 1.6 in \cite{N:2012} we obtain that $\Sigma$ is positive definite.
conclusions: $\Sigma$ is positive definite

nodes.name: Value is invariant to the time step $\Delta t$
nodes.statement: Moreover, when $\Delta t$ is changed $\Sigma$ is multiplied by a constant scalar, hence for fixed values of $n$, the delay ${D}$ and the ${\mathcal{H}}$ parameter, the value is invariant to $\Delta t$.
assumptions: for fixed values of $n$, the delay ${D}$ and the ${\mathcal{H}}$ parameter
conclusions: the value is invariant to $\Delta t$

nodes.name: Value decreases with the delay (numerical)
nodes.statement: The results, displayed in Fig. \ref{fig:value_vs_H}, show the decrease in the value as ${D}$ in increasing for both models.
conclusions: show the decrease in the value as ${D}$ in increasing for both models.

nodes.name: KMS model: value increases with correlation $\rho$ (numerical)
nodes.statement: As expected, for any delay ${D}$ the value is monotonically increasing with the correlations parameter $\rho$, hence longer delays can be tolerated with only a negligible drop in the value as $\rho$ increases.
conclusions: the value is monotonically increasing with the correlations parameter $\rho$, hence longer delays can be tolerated with only a negligible drop in the value as $\rho$ increases.

nodes.name: fBm with $H>1/2$: value increases towards 0 (numerical)
nodes.statement: For high ${\mathcal{H}}$ values (${\mathcal{H}}>0.5$), the increments are positively correlated hence the value increases with ${D}$ towards the maximum $0$.
conclusions: the increments are positively correlated hence the value increases with ${D}$ towards the maximum $0$.

nodes.name: fBm with $H=1/2$: value $-1$ for every delay
nodes.statement: For ${\mathcal{H}}=0.5$ we reduce to the independent Brownian motion case, hence the value drops to $-1$ regardless of the delay.
conclusions: the value drops to $-1$ regardless of the delay

nodes.name: fBm with $H<1/2$: non-monotonic dependence on $H$ (numerical)
nodes.statement: For low ${\mathcal{H}}$ values (${\mathcal{H}}<0.5$), the increments are negatively correlated hence the value increases, but the increase is non-monotonic in ${\mathcal{H}}$. The reason is that for very low ${\mathcal{H}}$ values the correlation between the increments decays faster to $0$ with their time distance, hence a delay results in almost complete loss of information regarding the current price.
conclusions: the increments are negatively correlated hence the value increases, but the increase is non-monotonic in ${\mathcal{H}}$.

nodes.name: Value increases towards zero with $n$ for fixed delay (numerical)
nodes.statement: For a fixed delay ${D}$, the value increases towards zero with $n$, this make sense since the continuous time fBm model leads to arbitrage (see for instance \cite{R:1997, C:2003}).
conclusions: the value increases towards zero with $n$

nodes.name: Value converges to a negative limit for fixed delay ratio (numerical)
nodes.statement: Increasing the delay ${D}_n$ with $n$ while keeping the ratio $\frac{{D}_n}{n}$ fixed amounts to refining the discretization towards the continuous limit with a fixed continuous delay $0 < {D} < T$. The value appears to converge to a negative number for this case (i.e. for $\frac{{D}_n}{n}=\frac{1}{64}$), with $-0.283$ for $n=256$ and $-0.228$ for $n=1024$.
assumptions: Increasing the delay ${D}_n$ with $n$ while keeping the ratio $\frac{{D}_n}{n}$ fixed
conclusions: The value appears to converge to a negative number for this case (i.e. for $\frac{{D}_n}{n}=\frac{1}{64}$), with $-0.283$ for $n=256$ and $-0.228$ for $n=1024$.
